ACCPPDE101: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate personal development, namely, being able to actively, consciously and ethically orientate oneself in relation to others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhance critical thinking and independent learning. It seeks to improve and develop academic writing and presenting skills and helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners.
BENECON111: Explore how individuals, firms, and societies make economic decisions. This course introduces key concepts from both microeconomics and macroeconomics, including markets, incentives, and the principles of supply and demand, and provides a foundation for analyzing real-world economic issues.
BENECON311: Investigate the role of government in the economy, focusing on how public policy influences efficiency and equity. The course covers taxation, public goods, externalities, and government spending. Combining theoretical models with empirical evidence, it evaluates how different policies affect societal welfare.
BENGATE102: Research Methods & Statistics introduces research design, operationalisation, measurement, sampling, surveys and experiments. Students study descriptive statistics, estimation, hypothesis testing and introductory regression using R and R Commander. A group project develops a research plan and instruments, collects and analyses data, and reports findings under research-ethics and privacy requirements.
ENSDELT311: Examines strategies and technologies towards a circular economy. Explores resource security and stewardship, develops lab skills and inorganic chemistry knowledge, and connects to themes at the Delta Climate Center.
ENSDELT312: This course examines sustainability through the lens of governance: “a process of rule-making and collective decision-making that includes both governmental and non-governmental actors in shaping public policy” (Fenger & Bekkers, 2016). Taking this lens, we ask questions such as how are sustainability policies on the local, national, and international level made and enforced? Which actors represent which interests, and which are most influential? How is public opinion on sustainability shaped, and how does public opinion shape politics? What, at the end of the day, determines effective policy for sustainability? By the end of this course, you will have gained a deep appreciation of the complexity of the governance dimension of sustainability, and have developed the theoretical and practical understanding to critically assess mainstream policy decisions.
ENSECOL112: Examines human-driven biodiversity loss and approaches to conservation. Students study habitat destruction, overharvesting, invasive species, climate change and extinction, followed by conservation planning and species management. A local threatened-species project investigates conservation status and protection measures and develops a public-awareness flyer.
ENSECOL211: Examines evolution from genes to populations, including its history, mechanisms and theoretical and practical study. It develops evolutionary explanations of biological diversity and change.
ENSECOL212: Focuses on basic principles of ecology. Studies how environmental conditions affect organisms and examines ecological principles governing individuals, populations, communities and ecosystems, including ecological modelling and applied case studies.
ENSECOL311: Marine Biology examines how marine ecosystems work and how people affect them. Students study ocean processes, marine microbes and habitats including estuaries, coasts and the deep sea. Seminars address issues such as fisheries, ocean acidification and plastic pollution. A multimedia project communicates a marine biology topic to a public audience.
ENSECOL312: Discusses environmental impacts of agriculture and explores sustainable agriculture approaches such as agroecology, organic farming, conservation agriculture, precision agriculture, sustainable livestock farming, agroforestry, permaculture, crop rotation, integrated pest management and sustainable supply chains.
ENSGATE101: Introduces sustainability through planetary boundaries and scientific tools for understanding human impacts on Earth systems. Students interpret graphs and uncertainty, build simple dynamic models, and study chemical and physical principles relevant to climate, energy and materials. A laboratory project makes and tests starch-based biopolymers.
ENSGATE201: Develops physical-science foundations for sustainability through waves, chemistry and materials science. Reflective work and a project apply these topics to analysing greenwashing.
ENSSUST111: Focuses on drivers and impacts of anthropogenic climate change on sea level, ocean acidification, ecology and society. Discusses adaptation and mitigation solutions, including renewable energy systems, carbon storage and climate‑adaptive planning, and examines climate governance and justice.
ENSSUST112: Teaches evaluation of environmental impacts of products, processes and services throughout their lifecycle. Emphasises strategic planning for a circular economy through hands‑on learning.
ENSSUST311: Teaches assessment of energy usage patterns and strategies for reducing consumption or transitioning to cleaner energy. Explores solar, wind and bioenergy solutions and includes technical and economic analysis; students deliver a report and presentation to a partner company.
ENSSUST315: Explores spatial engineering and geospatial technologies like GIS and remote sensing for addressing global challenges such as natural disasters, food shortages, resource decline and pollution. Emphasises hands‑on projects in disaster response, sustainable agriculture and environmental monitoring.
GOSGATE102: Law, Society & Justice examines legal, social and normative perspectives on law. Students compare legal traditions and study public and private law, human rights, justice, social control and change, race and gender. Case briefs, demand letters and mock trials develop legal reasoning, while a family-law topic supports the design of a socio-legal research proposal.
GOSHIST111: Provides a chronological overview of history from 1815 to the present. Discusses industrialisation, popular sovereignty and national self‑determination, and covers major economic, political and cultural developments including revolutions, world wars and the fall of communism.
GOSHIST112: Studies gender, storytelling and marginalised lives in the nineteenth- to twenty-first-century American context. Students examine slavery, community activism, representation and lived experience, using sources and projects that connect historical interpretation with contemporary questions.
GOSHIST312: Guides students through the full arc of historical inquiry, from formulating research questions to engaging critically with sources. Emphasises methodological rigour and interdisciplinary thinking and culminates in a substantial research paper.
GOSLAWJ212: Introduction to Public International Law examines its sources, theories, institutions and relationship to domestic law. Topics include responsibility, force, armed conflict, international crime, human rights, economic relations and environmental protection, followed by self-determination, Third World approaches, compliance and treaty politics. Case exercises and a research podcast develop legal reasoning and critical analysis.
GOSLAWJ311: Examines principles of property, tort and contract law and other selected areas of private law. It compares legal systems including Germany, France, England, China and the United States, and considers the social, economic and political pressures underlying legal principles.
GOSLAWJ312: Introduces the EU legal order. Studies institutions, framework, citizenship and the internal market using problem‑based exercises and guest lectures.
GOSPHIL212: Ethics examines moral reasoning through historical and contemporary theories and close philosophical reading. Students study utilitarianism, Kantian ethics, virtue ethics, contractarianism and feminist ethics, alongside Nietzsche, Murdoch and Nagel. Reflection and research essays develop interpretation, argument evaluation and an independent position on ethical theory or a practical ethical problem.
GOSPOLI111: Introduction to Political Philosophy examines political thought from classical antiquity to contemporary debates, including European and non-European thinkers. Students study views of human nature, society, rights and authority in historical context and compare their arguments with current political problems. Original texts, an essay and a group project develop interpretation and normative argument.
GOSPOLI112: Provides analytical tools to compare political systems and democracies. Examines phenomena like democratic backsliding, decline of political parties, rise of populism, media changes, non‑majoritarian institutions and globalization’s impact on domestic politics.
GOSPOLI212: Theory of International Relations introduces competing approaches to international relations and geopolitics, including realism, liberalism, Marxism, constructivism and critical theory. Students apply theories to historical and contemporary cases. A United Nations Security Council simulation develops country-position research, negotiation and collaborative resolution drafting.
GOSPOLI311: European Union Politics examines EU institutions, actors, integration and policymaking, including representation, legitimacy and decision-making. An empirical project investigates European Parliament committee amendments, relating MEP ideology and possible interest-group influence to amendment activity. Students plan the research, code amendments, assess salience and trace legislative processes.
GOSPOLI312: Investigates public policy in the context of globalization. Uses a case study on sugar to examine policy‑making phases and alternative conceptualisations across national and international arenas. Students write policy memos.
GOSPOLI313: Peace & Conflict examines conflict and approaches to peace through legal, sociological, political and historical perspectives. Structural inequality, identity and colonial legacies connect to international security, humanitarian law, human rights, peacebuilding and transitional justice. An interdisciplinary podcast, policy brief and research dossier develop analysis, while reflection examines how assumptions shape inquiry.
GOSSOCI111: Introduces concepts, theories and methods of sociology. Examines socio‑historical context of key authors like Marx, Weber, Durkheim and Du Bois, and encourages exploration of social problems related to race, gender and class through theoretical approaches and methodologies.
GOSSOCI212: Introduces qualitative research methodology. Covers designing questions, interpreting meaning and conducting small team projects, while reflecting on complexity and power dynamics in social research.
GOSSOCI215: Focuses on social movement theories and environmental justice. Uses case studies from the Environmental Justice Atlas and integrates perspectives such as feminism, anti‑colonialism, degrowth and environmental peacebuilding to encourage civic engagement.
GOSSOCI311: New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory studies civil society through critical, neo-functionalist and decolonial perspectives. Topics include trust, social capital, public spheres, solidarity, social movements and civil repair. An experience report connects engagement or observation to course concepts, while an individual project uses theoretical and empirical sources to analyse a civil-society organisation, movement or initiative.
HCBBIOM111: Introduces epidemiology and the evidence used in public health. It examines disease patterns, risks and changes over time, and how research can inform decisions about population health.
HCBBIOM311: Covers the science of drugs—their origin, composition, kinetics, therapeutic use and toxicity. Discusses drug targets, interactions and kinetics, enabling students to explain therapies in terms of molecular targets and physiological consequences.
HCBBIOM312: Explores fundamental processes in immunology such as recognition of self vs non‑self, lymphocyte receptor development and innate and adaptive immune responses. Examines host‑pathogen interactions, inflammation, tissue damage and immunopathology.
HCBBIOM313: Examines how normal organ-system function relates to disease. Students connect anatomy and physiology with symptoms, disease mechanisms, diagnosis, treatment and prognosis across digestive, cardiovascular, respiratory, renal, endocrine and nervous systems. Clinical cases and an imaginary-disease assignment develop coherent pathophysiological explanations.
HCBCOGN112: Neurobiology studies nervous systems and behaviour through comparative anatomy, evolution and physiology. Students examine animal behaviour, research models, welfare and research ethics, then connect biological rhythms and regulatory behaviour to sleep, lifestyle drugs, mood and eating disorders. Comparative-anatomy work and a literature-based report apply neurobiological concepts.
HCBCOGN212: Explores neural mechanisms behind perception and action. Examines how the brain processes sensory information and guides goal‑directed behaviour using methods from cognitive neuroscience and neuropsychology.
HCBCOGN311: Higher Order Functions deepens knowledge of neurophysiology, neuroanatomy and experimental cognitive neuroscience. Topics include attention, memory, emotion, cognitive control, social cognition, pain and consciousness. An attentional-blink experiment and a team research proposal develop engagement with empirical research, experimental design and ethical reflection.
HCBCOGN312: Psycholinguistics is the study of the neurobiological and psychological factors that enable us to acquire, use, and understand language. Modern research draws on cognitive psychology, neuroscience, and computer science to investigate how language is processed. The course focuses primarily, though not exclusively, on the neuroscience of language. Students examine theoretical and experimental issues in speech production and comprehension, language impairments, the relationship between thought and language, and the evolution and acquisition of language. They also gain hands-on experience with experimental approaches to the study of language and develop an understanding of human linguistic capacity as a subject of multidisciplinary research. Topics covered: What is language? Evolutionary aspects of language and animal communication; language and thought; aphasia; language acquisition; bilingualism; speech comprehension; semantics; reading and dyslexia; speech production.
HCBGATE101: Introduces the molecular and cellular foundations of life and biomedical science. Topics include biological molecules, cells and membranes, communication, metabolism, cell division, heredity, gene expression and biotechnology. Students analyse scientific experiments and papers through teaching contributions and a research-based mini-symposium, with additional topics selected with the class.
HCBGATE102: Explores why people behave as they do and how brain injuries affect mental processes. Discusses nature and nurture, introduces brain anatomy and psychological theories, and provides a gateway to cognitive science and clinical psychology.
HCBLIFE211: Provides foundation for practical applications in life science. Focuses on cellular biology of eukaryotes and prokaryotes, revisits concepts from introductory courses, examines current research and encourages evaluating reproducibility and modernising methods.
HCBLIFE212: Studies normal functioning of the human body, covering structure‑function relationships, energy handling, homeostasis, signalling, organ systems and integration of their functions.
HCBLIFE213: Explores the chemistry of life and biomolecules such as proteins, sugars, lipids and nucleic acids. Discusses metabolic pathways, the role of biomolecules in health and disease and applications in medicine, biotechnology and sustainability.
HCBLIFE214: Introduces biochemical and molecular laboratory work. Covers themes like blood, proteins, bacteria, DNA and bioinformatics and provides a foundation for clinical and biomedical research.
HCBLIFE311: Covers general and molecular pathology and genetics. Studies cell injury, death, inflammation, immunity, tissue repair, regeneration, fibrosis and neoplasia, examines genetic mutations and diseases, and discusses genetic testing and ethical considerations.
HCBPSYC211: Develops experimental-design knowledge and practical statistical analysis for health and behavioural research. Students choose, fit, diagnose and interpret multivariable models for group comparisons, categorical outcomes and latent constructs. R, primarily through R Commander, supports practical exercises; data-analysis papers and a poster connect research questions to appropriate models, assumption checks and clear reporting.
HCBPSYC212: Provides a deep dive into factors shaping mental health. Teaches critical thinking, explores the bio‑psycho‑social approach and covers mental disorders, research findings and assessment techniques.
HCBPSYC311: Uses a biopsychosocial approach to explore how biological, psychological and socio‑cultural factors influence health and illness. Covers theories, research and interventions and focuses on the role of psychological expertise in medical settings.
HCBPSYC312: Introduces concepts, methods and ethical issues in clinical psychological assessment and psychotherapy. Students compare approaches to assessment and treatment across age groups and learn to evaluate information critically.
HCBPSYC313: Advanced Research Methods & Statistics introduces systematic reviews and meta-analysis to synthesise results across studies. Students use R to conduct analyses, work with data structures and packages, estimate treatment effects and examine their consistency across studies. Presentations and active research tasks develop evidence-synthesis skills.
HCBPSYC314: Explores human development across the lifespan. Examines physical, cognitive, emotional and social changes from prenatal life to old age and develops critical thinking about factors influencing individual uniqueness.
MCCCOMM212: Examines how the climate crisis is communicated and contested. Analyzes texts, films, exhibitions, protest art, slogans and social media alongside theory and case studies, teaching students to dissect arguments and culminating in a project where students enter the debate.
MCCHEAM111: Introduction to Western Art History surveys Western art from late-medieval and Renaissance painting to contemporary practice. Students relate artists, styles and movements to social, religious, political and cultural change. Close examination of paintings develops visual analysis, while a term paper combines study of a painting on location with art-historical evidence.
MCCHEAM316: This course examines the history of art history as an academic discipline, tracing how scholars have understood and interpreted art from the sixteenth century to the present. Through critical readings of influential texts by figures such as Aby Warburg, Erwin Panofsky, Ernst Gombrich, Michel Foucault, and Jacques Derrida, students explore the major ideas and methodologies that have shaped the field. Topics include art and history, aesthetics, meaning and interpretation, authorship and identity, and the challenges of art history in a globalized world.
MCCLITR111: Introduction to Literary Studies introduces practical criticism and literary interpretation. Students examine what literature is, why it is read and studied, formal properties and the constructed character of texts. Fiction, poetry and drama are supplemented by contemporary nonfiction and basic film narration, developing critical terms, tools and techniques.
MCCLITR112: Provides a chronological overview of literature from the epic of Gilgamesh to post‑modernity. Reads literary and critical texts that explore human experience and teaches how to approach literature’s ambiguities and trace themes across ages.
MCCLITR212: Life & Travel Writing examines memoir, autobiography, diaries, personal essays, travel writing and digital self-presentation. Students explore memory, identity, autobiographical truth, ethics and cultural positioning through close reading and theory. A personal writing portfolio and an independent life-narrative project connect analysis with practice.
MCCMEDI311: Media & Race investigates storytelling, power, privilege, resistance and systemic racism in American history from the late nineteenth century to the present. Film, photographs, music and other media connect past and present. Students produce research-based podcasts exploring how media sustains oppression and supports resistance.
